title: The Lean Startup
author: Eric Ries
blurb: Eric Ries argues that most startups fail not because they can't build a product, but because they build something nobody wants. Drawing on his own experience, including the early struggles of the company IMVU, he proposes a scientific approach to entrepreneurship. A startup, he says, is any team creating something new under extreme uncertainty, whether in a garage or inside a large corporation. Instead of writing detailed plans, founders should treat their vision as a set of assumptions to test. They build a minimum viable product, measure how real customers respond, and learn whether to stay the course or pivot. Progress is measured by validated learning, not by vanity numbers. The book's core engine is the Build-Measure-Learn feedback loop, and the goal is to move through it as fast as possible, wasting less time, money, and effort.

lessons.t: Why Great Plans Build Unwanted Products
lessons.b: A startup is any team creating something new under extreme uncertainty, so following a detailed plan often means perfectly building something nobody wants.
issues: scene 2: The bottom takeaway 'Not size: how little anyone knows.' is crammed directly under the 'TWO FOUNDERS IN A GARAGE' caption, with almost no gap. The caption and the takeaway read as one cluttered block, and the garage drawing nearly touches its caption. (fix: Shrink the garage and the tower slightly, or move them up about 40px, so there is at least 40px of clear space between the captions and the takeaway line. Alternatively, move the takeaway line down to match its baseline in the other scenes (around y≈880 at 1600 scale).)

lessons.b: The true measure of a startup's progress is what it has proven about customers through real experiments, not how much it has built.
